translations.literal: When Liu Chong of Hedong invaded, Shizong summoned the chief ministers to discuss a personal campaign. Dao admonished him to stop. Shizong then said, "Early in Tang, bandits rose everywhere like bees, and Emperor Taizong personally pacified them all."
translations.idiomatic: When Liu Chong of Hedong invaded, Shizong summoned ministers to discuss campaigning in person. Dao urged him not to. Shizong said, "Early in Tang bandits rose everywhere, and Taizong pacified them himself."

sentences.zh: 」道奏曰：「陛下得如太宗否？

translations.literal: Dao memorialized, "Can Your Majesty equal Taizong?"
translations.idiomatic: Dao said, "Can Your Majesty equal Taizong?"

sentences.zh: 」世宗怒曰：「馮道何相少也！

translations.literal: Shizong said angrily, "How Feng Dao underestimates me!"
translations.idiomatic: Shizong snapped, "How Feng Dao underestimates me!"

sentences.zh: 」乃罷。

translations.literal: The discussion then ended.
translations.idiomatic: The discussion ended.

sentences.zh: 及世宗親征，不及扈從，留道奉太祖山陵。

translations.literal: When Shizong campaigned in person, Dao could not accompany him and was left to oversee the Founding Emperor's tomb rites.
translations.idiomatic: When Shizong campaigned in person, Dao could not accompany him and was left to oversee Taizu's tomb.

sentences.zh: 時道已抱疾。

translations.literal: By then Dao was already ill.
translations.idiomatic: By then Dao was already ill.

sentences.zh: 及山陵禮畢，奉神主歸舊宮，未及祔廟，一夕薨於其第，時顯德元年四月十七日也，享年七十有三。

translations.literal: When the tomb rites were finished he escorted the spirit tablet back to the old palace; before it could be installed in the ancestral temple, he died one night at his residence—on the seventeenth day of the fourth month of the first year of Xiande, at the age of seventy-three.
translations.idiomatic: When the tomb rites ended he escorted the spirit tablet to the old palace; before it could enter the ancestral temple he died one night at home—on the seventeenth day of the fourth month of Xiande 1, aged seventy-three.

sentences.zh: 世宗聞之，輟視朝三日，冊贈尚書令，追封瀛王，謚曰文懿。

translations.literal: When Shizong heard of it he suspended court audiences for three days, posthumously appointed him Director of the Department of State Affairs, enfeoffed him posthumously as Prince of Ying, and gave him the posthumous title Cultured and Virtuous.
translations.idiomatic: Shizong suspended court for three days, posthumously made him Director of the Department of State Affairs, Prince of Ying, and gave him the posthumous title Wényì.

sentences.zh: 道歷任四朝，三入中書，在相位二十餘年，以持重鎮俗為己任，未嘗以片簡擾於諸侯，平生甚廉儉。

translations.literal: Dao served four dynasties, entered the Secretariat three times, and held the chief ministership for more than twenty years. He took steadying the customs through weighty conduct as his charge, never troubling the regional lords with a single note, and was very frugal throughout his life.
translations.idiomatic: Dao served four dynasties, entered the Secretariat three times, and was chief minister for more than twenty years. He steadied custom through weighty conduct, never troubled the regional lords with a note, and lived very frugally.

sentences.zh: 逮至末年，閨庭之內，稍徇奢靡，其子吉，尤恣狂蕩，道不能制，識者以其不終令譽，鹹嘆惜之。

translations.literal: By his last years within the household he indulged luxury somewhat; his son Ji was especially unrestrained and dissolute, and Dao could not restrain him. Those who knew him, because his fine reputation did not last to the end, all sighed in regret.
translations.idiomatic: In his last years his household grew somewhat luxurious; his son Ji was especially dissolute, and Dao could not control him. Knowing men regretted that his fine reputation did not endure.

sentences.zh: （《五代史補》：馮道之鎮同州也，有酒務吏乞以家財修夫子廟，道以狀付判官參詳其事。

translations.literal: (Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties: When Feng Dao governed Tong Prefecture, a clerk of the wine monopoly asked to repair the Confucius temple with his family wealth. Dao handed the petition to the judge for deliberation.)
translations.idiomatic: (Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties: When Feng Dao governed Tongzhou, a wine-monopoly clerk asked to repair the Confucius temple with his family wealth. Dao referred the petition to his judge.)

sentences.zh: 判官素滑稽，因以一絕書判後云：「荊棘森森繞杏壇，儒官高貴盡偷安，若教酒務修夫子，覺我慚惶也大難。

translations.literal: The judge was by nature witty and therefore wrote a quatrain at the end of his decision: "Thorns grow thick around the apricot altar; noble Confucian officials all steal their ease. If the wine monopoly is made to repair the Master, I feel my shame and dread would be very hard indeed."
translations.idiomatic: The judge was witty and appended a quatrain: "Thorns grow thick around the apricot altar; Confucian officials all steal their ease. If the wine office repairs the Master, my shame would be hard to bear."

sentences.zh: 」道覽之有愧色，因出俸重創之。

translations.literal: When Dao read it he showed shame and therefore paid from his salary to rebuild the temple on a grand scale.
translations.idiomatic: Dao read it with shame and paid from his salary to rebuild the temple properly.

sentences.zh: 馮瀛王道之在中書也，有舉子李導投贄所業，馮相見之，戲謂曰：「老夫名道，其來久矣，加以累居相府，秀才不可謂不知，然亦名導，於禮可乎？

translations.literal: When the Prince of Yingzhou Feng Dao was in the Secretariat, an examination candidate named Li Dao presented his work. The chief minister saw him and jested, "This old man's name is Dao and has long been so; added to repeated tenure in the chief minister's office, the scholar cannot be said not to know it—yet you are also named Dao. Is that proper in ritual?"
translations.idiomatic: When Feng Dao was in the Secretariat, a candidate named Li Dao presented his work. Feng jested, "My name is Dao and has been for a long time; you cannot fail to know it, having come to the chief minister's office—yet you are also named Dao. Is that proper?"

sentences.zh: 」李抗聲對曰：「相公是無寸底道字，小子有寸底導字，何謂不可也！

translations.literal: Li answered boldly, "Your Excellency's character Dao has no inch at the bottom; this student's character Dao has an inch at the bottom—how can it be improper!"
translations.idiomatic: Li answered boldly, "Your Excellency's Dao has no 'inch' at the bottom; mine has an 'inch' at the bottom—how can it be improper!"

sentences.zh: 」公笑曰：「老夫不惟名無寸，諸事亦無寸，吾子可謂知人矣。

translations.literal: The duke laughed and said, "This old man not only has no inch in his name—he has no inch in anything. You may be called one who knows men."
translations.idiomatic: Feng laughed and said, "I have no inch not only in my name but in anything. You truly know men."

sentences.zh: 」了無怒色。

translations.literal: He showed not the least anger.
translations.idiomatic: He showed no anger at all.

sentences.zh: 馮吉，瀛王道之子，能彈琵琶，以皮為弦，世宗嘗令彈於御前，深欣善之，因號其琵琶曰「繞殿雷」也。

translations.literal: Feng Ji, son of the Prince of Yingzhou Feng Dao, could play the pipa with leather strings. Shizong once had him play before the throne and greatly admired it, therefore naming his pipa "Thunder Rolling Round the Hall."
translations.idiomatic: Feng Ji, Dao's son, could play the pipa with leather strings. Shizong had him play before the throne and greatly admired it, naming his pipa "Thunder Rolling Round the Hall."

sentences.zh: 道以其惰業，每加譴責，而吉攻之愈精，道益怒，凡與客飲，必使庭立而彈之，曲罷或賜以束帛，命背負之，然後致謝。

translations.literal: Because of his idle craft Dao often rebuked him, but Ji practiced all the more diligently, which made Dao angrier still. Whenever he drank with guests he made Ji stand in the courtyard to play; when the piece ended he might bestow a bundle of silk and order him to carry it on his back before thanking him.
translations.idiomatic: Dao often rebuked him for this idle craft, but Ji practiced all the harder, which angered Dao more. Whenever he entertained guests he made Ji play in the courtyard; when the piece ended he might give silk and make Ji carry it on his back before thanking him.

sentences.zh: 道自以為戒勖極矣，吉未能悛改，既而益自若。

translations.literal: Dao thought his admonition and discipline had reached the utmost, but Ji did not reform and afterward grew even more at ease.
translations.idiomatic: Dao thought he had disciplined him to the limit, but Ji did not reform and grew even more at ease.

sentences.zh: 道度無可奈何，嘆曰：「百工之司藝而身賤，理使然也。

translations.literal: Dao saw there was nothing to be done and sighed, "Among the hundred crafts, those who master an art remain low in station—it is the way of principle."
translations.idiomatic: Dao saw there was nothing to be done and sighed, "Among the hundred crafts, mastery of an art still means low station—that is how things are."

sentences.zh: 此子不過太常少卿耳。

translations.literal: This boy will rise no higher than Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices."
translations.idiomatic: This boy will rise no higher than Vice Director of Imperial Sacrifices."

sentences.zh: 」其後果終於此。）〉

translations.literal: In the end he indeed finished his career at that rank.)〉
translations.idiomatic: In the end he finished his career at exactly that rank.)〉

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：道之履行，郁有古人之風；

translations.literal: The historiographer says: In conduct and bearing, Dao richly possessed the air of the ancients;
translations.idiomatic: The historiographer says: In conduct and bearing, Dao had the air of the ancients;

sentences.zh: 道之宇量，深得大臣之禮。

translations.literal: in breadth of spirit he deeply grasped the rites of a great minister.
translations.idiomatic: in breadth of spirit he deeply understood a great minister's rites.

sentences.zh: 然而事四朝，相六帝，可得為忠乎！

translations.literal: Yet serving four dynasties and counseling six emperors—can this be called loyalty!
translations.idiomatic: Yet serving four dynasties and counseling six emperors—can this be called loyalty?

sentences.zh: 夫一女二夫，人之不幸，況於再三者哉！

translations.literal: For one woman to have two husbands is a person's misfortune—how much more when it happens a third time!
translations.idiomatic: One woman with two husbands is misfortune enough—how much more a third!

sentences.zh: 所以飾終之典，不得謚為文貞、文忠者，蓋謂此也。

translations.literal: Therefore in the rites honoring him at the end he was not given the posthumous titles Cultured and Upright or Cultured and Loyal—this is what is meant.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore he was not given the posthumous titles Wénzhēn or Wénzhōng in the rites of death—this is what is meant.
